title: "Gap Schemes: Power, Counter, Duo, Trap, Wham, Iso, and the Draw"
subtitle: "Why a guard runs sideways at the snap, and how an offense brings more blockers to one hole than the defense has defenders there"
description: "The gap (man/power) family of running plays, built from the ground up: down blocks, pullers and kick-outs; power and how it manufactures extra blockers at the point of attack; counter and the log block; duo; trap and wham; iso; the toss, the Lombardi sweep and pin-and-pull; the draw; how coaches choose gap or zone; and the pre-snap tells of a pulling lineman."
glossary:
  "Gap scheme": {def: "A family of running plays in which each blocker is assigned a man or a gap before the snap, chosen to give him a good angle (usually a down block), and extra blockers (pullers, a fullback, a tight end) are brought to a hole chosen in advance.", aliases: ["Man/power blocking"]}
  "Power": {def: "The signature gap-scheme run: the play-side linemen block down, the fullback or H-back kicks out the end man, and the backside guard pulls through the hole to lead on the play-side linebacker, while the backside end is left unblocked.", aliases: ["Power O"]}
  "Counter": {def: "A gap-scheme run that starts with the running back stepping away from the play, then pulls two backside blockers the other way: classically the guard, who kicks out the end man, and the tackle, who swings around the kick-out and leads through the hole (GT counter: guard and tackle).", aliases: ["Counter trey", "GT counter"]}
  "Duo": "A downhill gap-scheme run with no puller: two double teams drive the defensive tackles straight back, every other blocker takes the man on him, the double teams come off onto whichever linebacker fills, and the running back reads the Mike, hitting the gap he does not fill."
  "Trap": "A run in which the offense leaves a defensive lineman unblocked at the snap, lets him come across the line, and then blocks him from the side with a pulling lineman, so the ball can cut inside him."
  "Wham": "A trap block thrown by a tight end or H-back instead of a guard: the line leaves a defensive tackle unblocked, the lineman who would have blocked him releases to a linebacker, and the tight end or H-back comes across and hits the tackle from the side."
  "Iso": {def: "A run in which the linemen block the defensive linemen in front of them and the fullback leads through the hole onto a linebacker, 'isolating' that linebacker one-on-one against the fullback while the back reads the block.", aliases: ["Isolation"]}
  "Toss / sweep": "An outside run around the end: in a toss, the quarterback pitches the ball to a back already moving wide; in a sweep (handed or pitched), pulling linemen lead the back around the corner."
  "Pin-and-pull": "An outside-run blocking scheme in which each lineman with a defender in his backside gap blocks down on him (pins him) and each lineman without one pulls around to lead, so no one has to reach a defender lined up outside him."
  "Puller": "The lineman (or lineman pair) who pulls on a given play, usually from the backside, to kick out the end man or lead through the hole; the defense's best clue to where a gap run is going."
  "Log block": {def: "A block by a puller who meets an end man who has crashed inside: instead of kicking him out, the puller gets his head and body outside the defender and seals him in, and the ball carrier bounces outside the block. Some coaches call it a wrap, though others use 'wrap' for any puller who swings around a block and turns up.", aliases: ["Wrap"]}
  "Draw play": {def: "A run disguised as a pass: the line sets up to pass block and lets the rushers run upfield, the quarterback shows a drop, and the ball is handed to the back late, after the linebackers have turned to cover.", aliases: ["Draw"]}

import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, technique, style

GREEN = "#0f7a55"         # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]  # a ring colour for pullers: neither offense blue nor defense orange
OL_W = {"LT": -3.2, "LG": -1.6, "C": 0.0, "RG": 1.6, "RT": 3.2}


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line():
    """The five offensive linemen, labelled LT, LG, C, RG, RT."""
    return [O(k, k, -0.7, w, k) for k, w in OL_W.items()]


def te(side=1, key=None, label=None, d=-0.7):
    """An in-line tight end: Y on the right, U on the left."""
    key = key or ("Y" if side > 0 else "U")
    return O(key, "TE", d, side * 4.8, label or key)


def T(t, side=1):
    """Width of technique t on the offense's right (side=+1) or left (side=-1)."""
    return technique(t, side)


def dl(key, t, side, label=None):
    """A defensive lineman in technique t, labelled with the number."""
    return D(key, "DL", 1.0, T(t, side), label or t)


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, pull, path or run."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.2, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def pair_oval(fld, p, d, w, width, height=2.5, color=GREEN):
    """A faint oval around a double team (two blockers and their defender)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), width, height, fc=color, alpha=0.22, ec="none", zorder=1.5))
    fld.ax.add_patch(Ellipse((float(x), float(y)), width, height, fc="none", ec=color, lw=1.6,
                             ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=1.6))


def spot(fld, p, d, w, color=style.THIRD, ms=9):
    """Mark a point (the hole, the point of attack) with an X."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker="X", ms=ms, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=9)


def shade(fld, p, w0, w1, d0=-0.2, d1=6.5, color=style.THIRD, alpha=0.08):
    """Shade a rectangle from width w0 to w1 and depth d0 to d1 (the box, the play side)."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=color, alpha=alpha,
                               ec=color, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=0.8))


def dashed(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, lw=1.6, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed 'option' or 'intent' path through absolute (d, w) points, ending in an arrow or a block bar."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    if end == "arrow":
        fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))
    else:
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)
        v = np.array([xs[-1] - xs[-2], ys[-1] - ys[-2]])
        perp = np.array([-v[1], v[0]]) / np.linalg.norm(v) * 0.75
        fld.ax.plot([xs[-1] - perp[0], xs[-1] + perp[0]], [ys[-1] - perp[1], ys[-1] + perp[1]],
                    color=color, lw=lw + 0.6, zorder=6)


def clean(ax):
    """Box-zoomed diagrams: drop hash ticks and yard numbers, clip anything outside the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:   # yard numbers, not technique labels
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=5.8, ax=None, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a box-sized window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax)
    return fld


def subtitle(ax, text):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=9, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


# --- formations and fronts this chapter keeps coming back to -----------------------------------------
def i_form(side=1):
    """I-formation, 21 personnel, with the tight end on `side` (wide receivers outside the picture)."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.9, 0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.4, 0, "R"),
                     te(side)]


def pistol(y_side=0):
    """Pistol backfield (QB about 3.5 yards deep, RB behind him) with in-line tight ends:
    y_side=+1 the Y on the right, -1 the U on the left, 0 both."""
    off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -3.5, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0, "R")]
    if y_side >= 0:
        off.append(te(+1))
    if y_side <= 0:
        off.append(te(-1))
    return off


def over_front(side=1, safeties=True):
    """A 4-3 Over (named in 05-02), strength toward `side`: on the line a 5, a 1, a 3 and a 5, with the
    Sam standing up in a wide 9 outside the tight end; the Mike over the strong A gap, the Will over the
    weak B gap; two deep safeties."""
    s = side
    out = [dl("WE", "5", -s), dl("NT", "1", -s), dl("DT", "3", s), dl("SE", "5", s),
           D("SAM", "SAM", 1.0, s * 7.0, "S"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, s * 0.9, "M"),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -s * 2.5, "W")]
    if safeties:
        out += [D("FS", "FS", 10.5, -s * 7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 10.5, s * 7.0, "SS")]
    return out


def four_three_base(sam=True):
    """A four-man even front, 5-1-3-5 from the offense's left, with the 3-technique to the right."""
    out = [dl("BE", "5", -1), dl("NT", "1", -1), dl("DT", "3", 1), dl("PE", "5", 1),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.4, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 0.9, "M")]
    if sam:
        out.append(D("SAM", "SAM", 4.2, 6.4, "S"))
    return out


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web) for simulated plays ------------------------------------------
MARK_R = 0.6


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=()):
    """One moment of a simulated play on `ax`: markers, trails of on-screen players, rings."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.8, play.los + window[1] - 0.8)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.8, yhi - 0.8)]              # only players whose marker fits whole
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")
                & df["x"].between(play.los + window[0], play.los + window[1])]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"]))
        if r["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=9))
            continue
        lab = str(r.get("label", "") or "")
        if r["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.6)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r["x"], r["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), 0.95, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.5, zorder=7))
    return fld


def strip(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=6.5):
    """Numbered frame strip with a fixed, box-sized window, so markers stay legible in print."""
    df = tracking(play)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.55 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  " + ("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.2f} s".rstrip("0")),
                     fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.3 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, times, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), width_in=5.4):
    """Web version of the strip: the same panel at every frame, with the strip's notes as captions."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    df = tracking(play)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.4))
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()

    def update(fid):
        ax.clear()
        t = float(tmap[fid])
        panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        txt = ("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s")
        if notes:
            cur = [n for tt, n in zip(times, notes) if tt <= t + 1e-6]
            txt += ("   " + cur[-1]) if cur else ""
        ax.set_title(txt, fontsize=9, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=sorted(df["frameId"].unique()), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(play, times, **kw):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip(play, times, **kw)
        plt.show()
    else:
        kw.pop("ncols", None)
        kw.pop("width_in", None)
        video(play, times, **kw)
```

Third-and-1, the offense in a heavy formation with a fullback and a tight end, everyone in the
stadium knowing it will run. At the snap the right side of the offensive line fires *inward*, at an angle,
away from where the ball is going. At the same instant the left guard, who should be blocking the man in
front of him, turns and sprints sideways behind his own line. The fullback heads for the edge. The
running back waits a beat, then follows the guard into a hole just outside the tight end, and the guard
turns up into it and meets a linebacker head-on. Four yards, first down. The announcer says the offense
"just lined up and ran it right at them." True, but not the interesting part. Everyone knew where the ball
was going, so how did the offense get more blockers to that spot than the defense had defenders? The
answer is a family of plays coaches call **gap schemes**, and the guard who ran sideways is the key to
every one of them.

**You'll be able to:**

- Explain what makes a run a gap run, and the three parts of the classic gap run (down blocks, a kick-out
  and a puller) and why each exists.
- Recognize power, counter, duo, trap, wham, iso, the toss and sweep, pin-and-pull, and the draw on a
  broadcast, and draw each against a front you are shown by applying its blocking rules.
- Count the blockers and defenders at the point of attack and show how a gap scheme gains a man there,
  and what it pays for him.
- Say when a coach is likely to call a gap run rather than a zone run (the front, the personnel, the
  offensive line, the situation).
- Spot the pre-snap and first-step tells of a pulling lineman, and call the play's direction from them.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
- **[The Language of the Run Game](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)**: gaps A to D, technique numbers (a
  **3-technique** on a guard's outside shoulder, a **5** on a tackle's outside shoulder, a **1** shaded on the
  center), covered and uncovered linemen, play side and backside, the point of attack, hat math, and the eight
  core blocks, especially the **down block**, the **pull**, the **kick-out** and the **lead block**. This
  chapter is built from those words.
- Helpful but not required: [Zone Running](03-02-zone-running.qmd), the other great family of runs, which this
  chapter keeps comparing against; the [I-formation and the fullback](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd);
  and the [stance tells](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd) from How to Watch a Broadcast.
:::

**How to read the diagrams.** Offense is blue circles, defense orange squares, and the offense moves up the
page. *Left* and *right* are always the offense's left and right. LT, LG, C, RG and RT are the five offensive
linemen; Q is the quarterback, R the running back (HB a halfback, in the 1960s sweep), F a fullback, and Y and U
are tight ends on the right and left. H is the "move" player from [Formation Rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd):
an H-back in some diagrams, a slot receiver in others; each caption says which. Defensive linemen carry their technique number; S, M and W are the Sam, Mike
and Will linebackers; FS and SS the safeties; CB a cornerback; NB the nickel back. Lines ending in a short bar are
blocks; plain arrows are paths; the thick dark arrow is the ball carrier. **A purple ring marks a puller** (or another extra blocker), the
player this chapter wants you to follow. Most diagrams zoom in on the box, so the wide receivers (who keep the formation
legal, with seven men on the line) are often outside the picture.

## What makes a run a "gap" run?

In [Zone Running](03-02-zone-running.qmd) the offensive line asked one question after the snap: *who comes
into my area?* A gap scheme asks its question *before* the snap: *which man do I block, and from which angle?*
That is why gap blocking is also called **man** or **power** blocking. A [**gap
scheme**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-gap-scheme) (also [**man/power
blocking**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-power-blocking)) assigns each blocker a man or a gap in advance,
picks those assignments to give blockers good angles, and brings extra blockers to a hole the coach chose before
the snap.

That definition is the whole family resemblance, and it is worth reading twice, because it says nothing about
pulling. What makes a run a gap run is that **every blocker knows his man before the snap, and the hole is chosen in
advance**. Some gap runs pull two linemen; duo, iso and the draw pull nobody. They are still gap runs because their
blockers are assigned to men, not areas.

The *classic* gap run (power, counter, the sweep) is assembled from three parts you met in
[03-01](03-01-run-game-language.qmd), and the rest of the family drops or swaps one of them:

1. **Down blocks on the play side.** The linemen at the point of attack block the defender *inside* them,
   hitting him from the side. A down block is the easiest block in football to win, because the blocker has an
   angle and the defender is looking straight ahead. Down blocks build the inside wall of the hole.
2. **A kick-out on the end man.** Somebody (a fullback, an H-back, a pulling guard) hits the end man, the last
   defender on the line ([the kick-out](03-01-run-game-language.qmd); [Option Football](03-04-option-football.qmd)
   gives the full rule for finding him), from the inside and drives him toward the sideline. That builds the outside wall.
3. **A puller through the hole.** A lineman from the *backside* runs behind his own line, turns up between the two
   walls and blocks the first linebacker to show. He is the extra man.

Down blocks in, kick-out out, puller up through the middle. The hole is fixed and known to everyone on the offense,
including the running back, who does not have to find it; he has to *follow* someone into it. Contrast zone, where
the hole is wherever the wall cracks and the back's read is half the play.

The lineman who leaves his spot is the **[puller](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-puller)**: the guard (or tackle,
or both) assigned to pull on this play. He is the most important player on the field for you to find, because
**a puller runs to the hole**. The rest of this chapter is, in a sense, a catalogue of where pullers go.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Gap schemes exist to **win the numbers at the point of attack**. A defense can always put as many men in the box
as the offense has blockers, and usually one more ([hat math](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)). It cannot be equally
strong everywhere, though, and it has to line up before it knows where the ball is going. A gap scheme picks one
spot, then moves blockers there from elsewhere (a backside guard, a fullback) faster than the defense can move
defenders there. It pays for those men by leaving someone *away* from the play unblocked, and by being more
predictable: a pulling guard is a signpost. Every gap play in this chapter is a different answer to the same two
questions: *where do the extra blockers come from, and who is left free?*
:::

## Power: the play the whole family is built on

[**Power**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-power) (often called [**Power O**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-power-o)) is
the purest gap run, and the one to learn first. Here it is from the I-formation (a fullback behind the
quarterback and the tailback behind him) against a **4-3 Over**, a four-man front whose 3-technique lines up on the
side of the tight end (fronts are named and explained in [Even Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-02-even-fronts.qmd);
here it is just a set of numbers to block). Read it from the right, the play side, to the left. The hole is
**off-tackle**, the old name for "just outside the tackle": here that is the D gap, outside where the tight end
lined up (with no tight end on that side, the same play hits the C gap).



Walk through @fig-power one man at a time, because each assignment exists for a reason.

**The play-side wall: down blocks.** The tight end blocks *down* on the 5-technique inside him, and the right
tackle blocks down on the 3-technique inside *him*. Neither has to beat a defender lined up across from him; each
hits a man from the side, which is why gap teams love the down block. The right guard joins the tackle on the
3-technique for a moment, a [combo block](03-01-run-game-language.qmd), and then climbs to the backside linebacker,
the Will. Coaches teach these linemen one short rule, usually some version of *gap, down, backer*: if a defender
is in your inside gap, block him; if not, block down on the man over the lineman inside you; if nobody is there,
go to a linebacker.[^gdb] The rule means a play-side lineman never has to reach a man lined up outside him.

**The center blocks back.** The left guard is about to leave. The defensive lineman who was across from the
gap he leaves, here the 1-technique, would walk into the backfield, so the center blocks *back* on him, away from
the play. Because the 1 is shaded on the center's backside shoulder, it is another easy angle. This is not a
coincidence: coaches like to call power *toward* a 3-technique and *away* from a 1-technique for exactly these
angles.

::: {#cell-fig-power .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}

**The kick-out.** The fullback runs at the end man (here the Sam, standing up on the line outside the tight end in
a 9-technique) and hits him from the inside, driving him toward the sideline. The fullback does not need to win
big. If the Sam stays outside, the hole is inside him.

**The puller.** The left guard opens his hips toward the play with a short step back and out (coaches call it a
*bucket step* or a *skip pull*), sprints flat behind the center and the right side, staying tight to his teammates'
down blocks ("hug the down blocks"), and turns up into the hole, just outside the tight end's down block and inside
the kick-out, with his eyes inside for the first defender who appears. His man is the first linebacker who shows,
almost always the play-side linebacker (the Mike here) coming to fill. The running back follows him, aiming his
first steps at the tight end's outside hip and staying a step behind the guard's back, then cutting off the
guard's block.

**The backside.** With the guard gone, the left tackle **hinges**: he steps inside to close the B gap the guard
left, then swings back outside like a door closing, to keep the backside end from running straight down the line.
He does not try to drive the end anywhere. The end is the one defender power *chooses* not to block. That is the
deal at the heart of the play.

### Where power's extra blockers come from

Count the bodies, as in [hat math](03-01-run-game-language.qmd), and power's logic becomes arithmetic.

    fontsize=6.6)

The pulling guard and the fullback (purple rings) bring it to five for four. The price is the backside end (orange ring).](03-03-gap-and-power-runs_files/figure-html/fig-power-count-output-1.svg){#fig-power-count}

:::


@fig-power-count is the reason gap schemes exist. Before the snap, the side the offense wants to run to has three
blockers and four defenders. Run zone that way and somebody has to beat a man he is outnumbered against. Run power
and two blockers who started on the *other* side of the ball arrive at the point of attack within a second. Now count
the assignments, because that is where the extra man shows up:

- the Y takes the 5, the fullback takes the Sam, the pulling guard takes the Mike;
- the right tackle takes the 3, **and the right guard helps him**: that double team is the spare blocker.

Five blockers for four defenders means one man to spare, and power spends him in two installments: first as half of
a double team that drives the 3-technique off the ball, then, once the 3 is moving, as the blocker who climbs off it
to the backside linebacker, the Will. The defense cannot match that move, because its players learn where the ball
is going only when the snap shows them, while the offense knew before the huddle broke.

Now the whole box. The offense has seven blockers (five linemen, the Y and the fullback) against seven defenders (four
linemen and three linebackers). The center takes the 1, the right guard's climb takes the Will, and the left tackle's
hinge is a hat spent on nobody: he only closes the gap the guard left. So one defender is left over, and power makes
sure it is the backside end. **Power does not add a blocker to the box. It moves one, and the backside end is the
receipt.** It is betting that a defender who lines up farthest from the hole, and has to run down the line behind a
wall of bodies, will arrive too late. Most of the time he does. When the defense *knows* that and sends that end
screaming down the line at the snap, the offense has answers (a quarterback who keeps the ball and runs where the end
left, in [Option Football](03-04-option-football.qmd); a bootleg pass behind him, in
[Play-Action, Boots and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)).

The rest of the offense has jobs too, small but real. The quarterback opens, hands off and keeps carrying out a fake;
on many teams he then sells a bootleg away from the play, which is what keeps the free backside end honest. The wide
receivers, out of the picture here, block the men over them (usually a cornerback and a safety) so that the run does
not end at the second level. And the defense's usual answer to power, which [Run Fits and Box
Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd) builds in full, is to attack the
pullers: an end or linebacker who meets the kick-out or the puller *inside*, so the ball has to bounce outside to a fast
safety, plus that free backside end chasing from behind.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Power works because the offensive line is bigger and stronger." Strength helps, but the play is designed so that
nobody has to win a fair fight. The down blocks hit men from the side; the kick-out hits the end man from inside,
where he is not looking; the puller arrives as an extra man. What power needs is not the biggest line but a line
that can *pull*: a guard who can run ten yards laterally and still hit a linebacker. That is why gap-scheme teams
prize athletic guards as much as heavy ones.
:::

The "O" in Power O is not explained consistently from one coaching tree to the next, so do not read much into it.

Walk the rules and the play draws itself. On the play side nothing changes in principle: the Y has a man in his inside
gap (the 5), so he blocks down; the right guard has the 1 in his gap, so he blocks down on him; the right tackle has
nobody in his gap and nobody over the guard beside him, so the third word of the rule sends him to a linebacker, the
backside one. The problem is the backside. The center can block back on a 1-technique shaded on him, but a 3-technique
sits outside the guard, two gaps away, and a center cannot get there. If the left guard pulled anyway, the 3 would be
loose in the backfield, right in the path of the puller and the back. So the offense keeps the guard home and pulls the
tackle, a version many coaches call **dart** or "tackle power."[^dart] The price is distance: the tackle has farther to
run, so dart needs an athletic tackle. Other answers to the same front are to check to a different run or to run power
the other way, at the 3.

## Counter: the same blocks, a different first step

Power has one weakness that defenses learn quickly: the running back's first step points at the hole, and so does
the puller. A linebacker who reads both is moving toward the hole before the guard gets there.
[**Counter**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-counter) attacks that reflex. It starts with the back stepping the
*wrong* way, and it pulls **two** backside blockers the right way: classically the guard, who kicks out the end man,
and the tackle, who *wraps*, swinging around the guard's kick-out and up through the hole as the lead blocker. (The
tackle is not throwing a log block here; "wrap" is a word coaches use loosely, as the log-block section below explains.)
The guard-and-tackle version is called [**GT counter**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-gt-counter), GT for guard and
tackle, and its most famous name is the [**counter trey**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-counter-trey) of Joe Gibbs's
Washington teams. Where "trey" came from is not well documented; treat it as a name rather than a description.

Compare @fig-counter with @fig-power. The play side follows the *same rules*, though the picture differs because the
front does: there is no tight end or Sam on the right here, so the right tackle blocks down on the 3-technique, the
right guard climbs to the backside linebacker, the center blocks back on the 1, and the end man is the 5-technique
himself. What changed is *who supplies the extra men*. Instead of a fullback for the kick-out, the backside guard does
it; instead of the guard leading through the hole, the backside tackle does. Two linemen leave the backside, so
something has to fill the space they left: here the U tight end blocks the backside end, and in other versions an
H-back fills, or the end is simply left for the quarterback to read.

Count it the way you counted power. The defense has six in the box (four linemen, two linebackers) and keeps two
safeties deep. The offense has six blockers: five linemen and the U. RT on the 3, the pulling guard on the 5, the
pulling tackle on the Mike, the right guard on the Will, the center on the 1, the U on the backside end: a hat on every
defender in the box. Against this two-high front, counter does not even leave the backside end free; the free men are
the two safeties, ten yards away, and the back's job is to make them miss.

And the running back's first step goes *away*. That counter step, a single lateral jab in the wrong direction, is the
whole trick. Linebackers are taught to read the back and the guards. On counter the back says *left* while the guards
say *right*, and a linebacker who trusts his eyes takes one false step toward the back, which is all the pulling tackle
needs to arrive first. In the simulation the Mike's first steps go toward the back's jab (frame 1), and by the time
he corrects, the tackle is already in the hole.

Counter has a price too. Two pullers take longer to arrive than one, so the back's counter step is partly a way to buy
time: the ball cannot hit the hole before the blockers do. If a defensive lineman penetrates into the space the pullers
must run through, he can wreck both pullers at once. And a defense that keys the *guards* (watches them for its cue)
and ignores the back is not fooled at all, which is why offenses mix counter with power, zone, and fakes of all of them.

::: {#cell-fig-counter .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def counter_play():
    """GT counter right from the shotgun, U tight end on the left, against a 5-1-3-5 even front."""
    off = line() + [te(-1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -1.6, "R")]
    dfn = [dl("BE", "5", -1), dl("NT", "1", -1), dl("DT", "3", 1), dl("PE", "5", 1),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 4.6, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.6, 1.4, "M"),
           D("FS", "FS", 11.0, -7.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 7.5, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    # defense: the end rushes upfield, the tackles fight their blocks, the linebackers read and flow
    go_to(p, "PE", (-0.2, 4.7), "path", speed=2.6)                       # upfield ...
    go_to(p, "PE", (0.6, 7.7), "path", speed=2.6, delay=0.85)           # ... and kicked out
    go_to(p, "DT", (1.0, 1.7), "path", speed=1.2, delay=0.2)             # driven inside by the down block
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.9, -0.9), "path", speed=0.6)
    go_to(p, "BE", (0.6, -4.3), "path", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, -0.5), "path", speed=3.2)                     # first steps follow the back's jab
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.2, 3.1), "path", speed=3.6, delay=0.15)          # then fills toward the hole
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.9, -2.9), "path", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (3.0, 0.4), "path", speed=3.5, delay=0.2)
    go_to(p, "SS", (7.0, 6.0), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.6)
    go_to(p, "FS", (9.0, -2.5), "path", speed=3.0, delay=0.6)
    # offense
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.9), via=[(-0.4, 3.1)], speed=2.0)             # down on the 3
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.6, 2.3), speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "RG", (2.2, 0.0), via=[(-0.2, 1.3)], speed=2.4)             # up to the Will
    go_to(p, "C", (0.15, -0.25), via=[(-0.5, -0.3)], speed=1.6)          # back block on the 1
    go_to(p, "U", (0.0, -3.8), via=[(-0.5, -4.6)], speed=1.6)            # fills for the pulled tackle
    go_to(p, "LG", (-0.6, 4.3), "pull", via=[(-1.6, -1.5), (-1.9, 2.8)], speed=5.3)   # kick out the end
    go_to(p, "LG", (-0.1, 6.8), speed=2.4)
    go_to(p, "LT", (2.4, 3.6), "pull", via=[(-1.5, -3.0), (-2.6, -1.6), (-2.6, 2.6), (-0.6, 4.4)], speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-5.2, 0.3), "path", speed=0.5)                       # rides the mesh
    go_to(p, "RB", (-5.2, -2.7), "run", speed=4.0)                       # counter step away
    go_to(p, "RB", (5.4, 5.0), "run", speed=6.0, delay=0.4, via=[(-4.4, -0.1), (-3.0, 2.6), (-0.6, 4.7)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=1.02)
    return p

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Washington, 1983 season"}
**The play:** Gibbs installed the counter trey in his first season, 1981, and ran it for a decade. The Washington
version pulled the left guard and left tackle (Russ Grimm and Joe Jacoby, two of the original
[Hogs](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)) to the right, while the right side blocked down as if the play were going left
and the back jabbed left before taking the handoff going right. Gibbs himself credited Tom Osborne's Nebraska teams:
his staff watched Nebraska film, liked what Osborne's line was doing, "so, we stole it." (Nebraska's counter is usually dated
to its 1982 season, a year after Gibbs arrived, so accounts of exactly which came first differ.)[^trey]

**The season:** in 1983, behind that line, 34-year-old John Riggins ran for 1,347 yards and 24 rushing touchdowns, then
the NFL record, for a team that went 14–2.[^riggins]

**What to notice:** on any Washington run from those seasons, ignore the ball and watch numbers 68 and 66 on the left
side. If both of them pull right, it is the counter trey, and you can call the hole (just outside the right tackle's
down block) before the back even turns back toward it.
:::

Counter comes in many flavors that keep the same skeleton, and playbooks name them by the pullers: GT counter pulls the
guard and tackle; GH or GY counter pulls the guard and an H-back or tight end (Y), which spares the tackle the long trip
and leaves him home to block the backside end.[^counternames] Some teams run it from the shotgun with the quarterback reading the
backside end instead of blocking him ([Option Football](03-04-option-football.qmd) covers those reads); some run it *as*
the quarterback's own run. When you see two blockers pull the same way *after the back has stepped the other way*,
think counter first.

### New block: the log

Every kick-out has an assumption hidden in it: that the end man will stay outside, where there is room to drive him
toward the sideline. Defenses do not always oblige, and [Zone Running](03-02-zone-running.qmd) already gave you their two
plans for meeting a blocker. With **box** (also called *squeeze*), the end squeezes down inside as the man beside him
blocks down, but keeps his outside arm free, so the ball has to go back *inside* him. With **spill**, the end attacks
the kick-out man's *inside* half with his outside shoulder (coaches call this *wrong-arming* or wrong-shouldering the
blocker), giving up the outside on purpose to pile up the hole, so the ball has to bounce *outside* to a teammate
waiting there. Choosing between them is a big part of
[Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

So the kick-out man reads the end as he arrives. He aims for the end's inside number. If he can get his head inside
the defender, he kicks him out and the ball goes inside. If the end has crashed so far inside (a hard squeeze, or a
spill player wrong-arming) that the blocker cannot get his head inside, there is no "out" left to kick him toward, so he
throws a [**log block**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-log-block): he takes the defender's *outside* shoulder, gets
his head and body outside him, seals him in, and the ball carrier bounces outside the block. Some line coaches call
this *wrapping* or *logging* the end; others use [**wrap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wrap) for any puller who
swings around a block in front of him and turns up, like the counter tackle above. Either way, **the defender decides
where the hole is, and the blockers and the back read him**.

Who reads him depends on the play. On power the kick-out man is the fullback or H-back, and the pulling guard turns up
off whatever the fullback does; on counter the kick-out man is the pulling guard, and the tackle behind him does the
same. The lead puller always goes to the hole the kick-out man leaves.

::: {#cell-fig-kick-or-log .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def ghost(f, p, frm, to, label="5"):
    """The end man's pre-snap spot (dashed outline) and an orange arrow to where he is when the puller arrives."""
    x, y = _P(f, p, *frm)
    f.ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((float(x), float(y)), 4, radius=0.75 * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4, fc="none",
                                  ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=5))
    f.ax.text(float(x), float(y), label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.7, zorder=5)
    dashed(f, p, [frm, to], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)


def kl_play(crash):
    """Counter right, the moment the pulling guard reaches the end man: he stayed wide, or he crashed inside."""
    end = (0.45, 4.35) if crash else (-0.4, 5.7)
    off = [O("C", "C", -0.7, 0.0, "C"), O("RG", "RG", -0.7, 1.6, "RG"), O("RT", "RT", -0.7, 3.2, "RT"),
           O("LG", "LG", -0.7, -1.6, "LG"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, -0.6, "R")]
    dfn = [dl("DT", "3", 1), D("PE", "DL", *end, "5")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 2.75), via=[(-0.3, 3.05)])                     # RT and RG double the 3
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.3, 1.85), via=[(-0.3, 1.75)])
    if not crash:            # the end stayed outside: hit him from the inside and drive him out
        go_to(p, "LG", (-1.0, 4.75), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.0), (-2.1, 1.6), (-2.0, 3.6)])
        go_to(p, "RB", (4.4, 4.3), "run", via=[(-3.8, 0.6), (-2.4, 3.0), (-0.2, 4.0)])
    else:                    # the end crashed inside: get outside him and seal him in (log)
        go_to(p, "LG", (0.3, 5.35), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.0), (-2.1, 1.6), (-2.2, 4.4), (-1.0, 6.2)])
        go_to(p, "RB", (4.4, 7.3), "run", via=[(-3.8, 0.6), (-3.0, 3.6), (-2.0, 6.4), (0.4, 7.0)])
    p.highlight("LG", color=PURPLE)
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.6))
for ax, crash, ttl in [(axes[0], False, "End stays wide: kick him out"), (axes[1], True, "End crashes inside: log him")]:
    p = kl_play(crash)
    f = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-2.8, 9.0), window=(-6.2, 5.4), title=False)
    ghost(f, p, (1.0, 4.0), (p.players["PE"].d + (0.35 if crash else 0.45), p.players["PE"].w + (0.75 if crash else -0.5)))
    subtitle(ax, ttl)

        say(f, p, -4.4, 5.6, "puller gets his\nhead outside\nand seals in", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)
    else:
        say(f, p, 3.2, 6.9, "ball cuts\ninside him", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
        say(f, p, -4.4, 5.6, "puller hits him\nfrom the inside\nand drives out", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)

This is why gap runs are not as rigid as they look on a whiteboard. The *assignments* are fixed before the snap; the
*hole* still moves a yard or two depending on what the end man does, and the back's eyes are on the kick-out man's
helmet. **The back runs to the side the helmet is on**: head inside the defender (a kick-out), cut inside; head outside
him (a log), bounce outside.

## Duo: power without a puller

Not every gap run pulls anybody. [**Duo**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-duo) is the downhill, no-frills member of
the family, and the one that manufactures nobody: two double teams (hence the name) drive the two defensive tackles
straight back, every other blocker takes the man in front of him, and nobody moves sideways. It is still a gap run,
because every blocker knows his man before the snap and the back is aimed at a hole chosen in advance. It looks like [inside zone](03-02-zone-running.qmd) for the
first instant, which is part of the point, but the footwork is different: zone linemen step *sideways* toward the play;
duo linemen step *forward*, into the defenders, and the double teams stay on the defensive tackles longer, trying to move
them back a yard or two before anyone climbs.

Where do duo's extra blockers come from, if nobody pulls? From the **defense's own choice**. Look at the box in
@fig-duo: six defenders against six blockers, with two safeties sitting 12 yards deep. Against a defense that keeps
two safeties high to protect against the pass (a [light box](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)),
the offense already has a hat for every hat, and it does not need to manufacture one. What it needs is *movement*,
someone driven backward so the back can fall forward for four yards, and two double teams on the two biggest defenders
are the most direct way to get it. Duo does not fool anyone. It is a bet that your five linemen and a tight end can move
their six, and that your running back can make the last man miss.

The running back's job is the subtle part. Since the linemen block the defensive linemen first and climb late, the
linebackers are, for a beat, unaccounted for, and the back is the one who "blocks" them with his path. The double teams
own them: the double on the 1 owns the Will, the double on the 3 owns the Mike, and whichever way a backer attacks
decides which lineman comes off to meet him. The back presses the double teams, aiming at the A gap between them, and
watches the Mike. If the Mike fills the A gap, the back bounces to the B gap off the double on the 3; if the Mike fills
outside, the back stays in the A gap. It is a read, like zone's, but a vertical one: the back is choosing which
side of a double team to run past, not whether to cut back across the field.

That difference is also how you tell duo from [inside zone](03-02-zone-running.qmd) on the broadcast, where the two look
alike for a heartbeat (both start with double teams and no pullers). Watch the line's first step from the high end-zone
camera: on inside zone every lineman steps sideways toward the play together, so the whole line drifts; on duo the
linemen step straight ahead and the double teams stay on the tackles longer, so the line *surges* without drifting. Then
watch the back: on duo he runs straight downhill at the doubles; on inside zone his path angles toward the play side
before he reads.

Duo's trade is plain. It needs blockers who can move people straight back, and it does nothing to the numbers: against
a seventh or eighth defender in the box, there is nobody to block him. That makes duo a **two-high play**, and its rise
in the last decade tracks the rise of two-high defenses: when defenses take a safety out of the box to stop the pass,
offenses answer by running straight at the six who are left. NFL Next Gen Stats measured split-safety coverage on 42% of
plays in 2025, the most since its tracking began in 2018, which tells you how many light boxes NFL offenses now see.[^twohigh]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Tennessee Titans 2020"}
**The season:** Derrick Henry carried 378 times for 2,027 yards and 17 touchdowns, all league highs, and became the eighth
player to run for 2,000 yards in a season. The offense, coordinated by Arthur Smith, mixed outside zone with a heavy diet of
duo, often from two- and three-tight-end sets.[^titans]

**What to notice:** Henry is listed at 6-foot-2 or 6-foot-3 and about 250 pounds, and, by every account, at his best running *downhill*, building speed straight at the
defense rather than stopping and starting. Duo gives him exactly that: on the snap, watch the two double teams surge forward,
then watch Henry press between them, find the linebacker, and run through the gap the linebacker did not fill. Count how often
his first contact comes four or five yards past the line.
:::

## Trap: let him in, then hit him from the side

[**Trap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trap) is one of the oldest plays in football and still one of the most
satisfying to watch, because it uses a defender's aggression against him. The offense leaves a defensive lineman
*unblocked* at the snap. He feels nobody in front of him and does what he is paid to do: he charges across the line.
Then a pulling lineman, usually the backside guard on a short pull, hits him from the side, where he is not looking,
and the ball carrier cuts just inside him.

::: {#cell-fig-trap .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def trap_play(wham=False, static=False):
    """Trap right (the LG pulls) or wham right (an H crosses the formation), from the pistol.
    static=True: blocks drawn to the defenders' pre-snap spots, for the assignment diagram;
    static=False: the simulated play, with blockers and defenders meeting where they really would."""
    off = pistol(y_side=1 if wham else -1) + ([O("H", "TE", -1.5, -6.4, "H")] if wham else [])
    p = Play(off, four_three_base(sam=wham), los=35, to_go=None)
    t_hit = 1.45 if wham else 0.9
    trapper = "H" if wham else "LG"
    pull_via = [(-1.8, -4.4), (-1.9, 0.6)] if wham else [(-1.6, -1.2), (-1.9, 0.6)]
    if static:
        go_to(p, "DT", (-0.6, 2.6), "path", speed=2.0)                    # the 3 is let through
        go_to(p, trapper, (0.15, 1.9), "pull", via=pull_via, speed=6.0)   # ... and trapped from the inside
        mike, will, rg, lg_or_lt = (3.9, 0.9), (3.9, -2.2), (3.9, 0.9), (3.9, -2.2)
    else:
        go_to(p, "DT", (-0.9, 2.55), "path", speed=1.95 / (t_hit - 0.1))  # the 3 is let go and comes upfield
        go_to(p, "DT", (-0.05, 4.45), "path", speed=1.75, delay=0.1)       # ... until he is hit from the side
        go_to(p, trapper, (-1.3, 1.85), "pull", via=pull_via, speed=6.0 if wham else 5.0)
        go_to(p, trapper, (-1.0, 3.2), speed=1.5)                         # drive him out
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.75, -0.1) if wham else (3.7, 0.4), "path", speed=2.5, delay=0.3)
        go_to(p, "PE", (1.3, 5.6), "path", speed=1.0, delay=0.2)
        go_to(p, "WILL", (4.1, -1.9), "path", speed=2.5, delay=0.3)
        mike, will, rg, lg_or_lt = None, None, ((2.5, 0.1) if wham else (2.45, 0.7)), (2.8, -1.45)
    go_to(p, "C", (0.35, -0.3), via=[(-0.45, -0.15)])                     # back block on the 1
    go_to(p, "RG", rg, via=[(-0.2, 1.1)])                                 # inside release to the Mike
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.4, 4.2) if static else (0.5, 4.75), via=[(-0.3, 3.35)], speed=1.6)   # base the 5
    if wham:
        go_to(p, "LG", lg_or_lt, via=[(-0.2, -1.4)])                      # climbs to the Will
        go_to(p, "LT", (0.35, -3.6) if static else (0.0, -3.45), via=[(-0.3, -3.35)])    # the backside end
        go_to(p, "Y", (0.6, 6.2) if static else (3.3, 6.2), via=[(0.2, 5.3)] if not static else [(-0.2, 5.6)])  # the Sam
    else:
        go_to(p, "LT", lg_or_lt, via=[(-0.2, -2.9)])                      # inside release to the Will
        go_to(p, "U", (0.35, -4.4) if static else (0.05, -4.7), via=[(-0.3, -4.75)])     # down on the end
    go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, 1.4), "run", delay=0.55 if wham else 0.15, speed=6.0,
          via=[(-4.3, 0.5), (-1.7, 0.95), (0.6, 1.25)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.95 if wham else 0.5)
    p.highlight(trapper, color=PURPLE); p.highlight("DT", color=style.DEFENSE)
    return p, trapper, t_hit


T_TRAP = {False: 1.5, True: 1.9}          # the moment the right-hand panel shows


def trap_figure(wham=False):
    """Left: the static assignments. Right: the simulated play just after the trap block lands."""
    p, trapper, t_hit = trap_play(wham)
    ps, _, _ = trap_play(wham, static=True)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
    lat, win = ((-8.0, 8.0) if wham else (-7.6, 7.6)), (-7.9, 6.6)
    f = draw(ps, ax=axes[0], lateral=lat, window=win, title=False)
    point_to(f, ps, (-4.6, 3.6), (-1.4, 0.9), ("H" if wham else "LG") + " crosses and\ntraps the 3\nfrom inside",
             color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)
    point_to(f, ps, (3.0, 4.9), (1.0, 2.35), "3: left\nunblocked", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
    subtitle(axes[0], "The assignments")
    t = T_TRAP[wham]
    panel(axes[1], p, tracking(p), t, lat, win,
          rings=((trapper, PURPLE), ("DT", style.DEFENSE), ("RB", style.THIRD)))
    subtitle(axes[1], f"{t:.1f} s after the snap")
    fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.8)


trap_figure(wham=False)
plt.show()
```

Left, the assignments: nobody blocks the 3-technique (orange ring); the right guard and left tackle release inside him to the linebackers, the center blocks back on the 1, and the left guard (purple ring) makes a short pull behind the center and traps the 3 from the inside. Right, the simulated play 1.5 seconds after the snap: the 3 has charged a yard into the backfield and been driven back out toward the sideline, and the back (green ring) is through the hole inside him.](03-03-gap-and-power-runs_files/figure-html/fig-trap-output-1.svg){#fig-trap}
:::
:::


Why would anyone *invite* a defender into the backfield? Because of what it does to the rest of the line. With the
3-technique left alone, the right guard does not have to block him and can go straight to the Mike, and the left tackle
can go straight to the Will: in @fig-trap both linebackers are blocked within a second, which is hard to do on most runs.
And the defender who was left alone is beaten by geometry rather than strength. A lineman charging upfield has his
shoulders pointed at the quarterback; a guard arriving from the side hits him where he cannot anchor, and the harder he
charged, the farther past the hole he ends up.

Trap is a **counter-punch to penetration**. It is most dangerous against an aggressive, one-gap defensive tackle, the
kind of 3-technique who lives in the backfield, and against defenses that slant hard at the snap. It is least dangerous
against a disciplined lineman who reads the guard: if the guard in front of him releases *inside* instead of blocking
him, a well-coached tackle knows the trap is coming, squeezes down, and closes the hole before the trapper gets there.
Coaches answer with [constraint plays](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd) (plays designed to
punish a defender for doing his job too well) such as the *influence* trap, in which the lineman in front of the trapped man pretends
to pass-block, inviting the defender upfield, before the trap hits him.

The trap's pedigree runs back to the earliest days of the T-formation. Paul Brown's Cleveland teams of the late 1940s, with
quarterback Otto Graham and fullback Marion Motley, were famous for two plays that turn a defense's aggression against it:
the trap and the draw (which closes this chapter).[^motley]

## Wham: the trap a tight end throws

[**Wham**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wham) is the same idea with a different trapper. The line leaves a defensive
tackle unblocked, the guards climb to the second level, and a tight end or H-back comes across the formation and hits the
tackle from the side.

::: {#cell-fig-wham .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
trap_figure(wham=True)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Wham right: a trap thrown by an H-back. Left, the assignments: again nobody blocks the 3-technique. The H, lined up off the line on the left, runs flat across the formation and hits him from the inside. Because no guard pulls, both guards climb to the linebackers, and the Y goes out to the Sam. Right, the simulated play 1.9 seconds after the snap: the 3 has been whammed out of the hole, both guards and the Y are on linebackers, and the back is through the hole inside the block.](03-03-gap-and-power-runs_files/figure-html/fig-wham-output-1.svg){#fig-wham}
:::
:::


Swapping a guard for a tight end does not change the head count; it changes *who is left on the line*. Compare the two
figures (ignore the wham's extra Sam and the Y who blocks him, which only reflect the different personnel). On the trap,
one of the five linemen is the trapper, so the line has a hole in it where the guard used to be, and a linebacker who
watches the guards sees one pull and knows where the ball is going. On the wham, the trapper comes from outside the line,
so all five linemen stay home or go straight ahead: no gap is vacated for a backside defender to shoot through, both
guards can climb to the linebackers at once, and a linebacker reading the guards sees them come straight at him, as on a
base run. The obvious objection is size: a 250-pound tight end against a 300-pound tackle. The answer is the angle. The
tackle is charging upfield, looking at the quarterback, and the tight end has a running start into his hip. It is, as
Chris B. Brown put it, a surprisingly simple block, because the defender is so focused on getting into the backfield that
he never sees it coming.[^wham]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Francisco 49ers 2011"}
**The play:** in Week 6 of the 2011 season at Detroit, Jim Harbaugh's 49ers (offensive coordinator Greg Roman) faced Ndamukong
Suh, one of the most destructive interior linemen in football. Their plan was to *not* block him: on wham runs, the line left
Suh alone and released to the linebackers, and tight end Delanie Walker came across and hit him from the side as he charged
into the backfield, with Frank Gore running past.[^wham-sf]

**What to notice:** wham is easiest to spot from the end-zone replay. Look for a defensive tackle who comes free through the
line untouched, *too* free, and then a tight end arriving at his hip from the other side of the formation. Then look at the
second level: on a well-blocked wham, every linebacker has a blocker on him.
:::

Roman took the same toolkit (power, counter, trap and wham, plus fullbacks and extra tight ends) to Baltimore, where it
became half of the most productive rushing offense in NFL history; the film room on the 2019 Ravens is below.

## Iso: the fullback against the linebacker

[**Iso**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-iso), short for [**isolation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-isolation), is
the simplest run in this chapter. Every lineman blocks the defensive lineman on him, the uncovered lineman takes the
backside linebacker, and the fullback runs through the hole and blocks the play-side linebacker: one man, alone, against a
fullback with a running start.

That leaves the Mike (orange ring) 'isolated': the fullback (purple ring) leads through the strong-side A gap (green X) and meets him as he fills. Two deep safeties, not shown, are the only defenders nobody blocks.](03-03-gap-and-power-runs_files/figure-html/fig-iso-output-1.svg){#fig-iso}

Iso's logic is a clean version of hat math. Against a seven-man box (four linemen, three linebackers), the offense has seven
blockers: five linemen, a tight end and a fullback. Every defender gets a hat, and the one matchup the play depends on is the
fullback against the Mike. Where it hits is decided by the front: iso usually aims at a *bubble*, an open gap or an
uncovered lineman where the nearest defender is a linebacker rather than a defensive lineman, so the fullback can get to
him. In @fig-iso the strong A gap is open because the 1 is shaded to the other side of the center and the 3 lines up
outside the right guard; the center and guard only have to turn their men away from it. Against this front the offense
could also run iso weak, over the uncovered left guard, at the Will.

The trade is that iso gains nothing in the numbers and moves nobody sideways; it is a straight contest. Its virtues are speed and
simplicity: the ball hits fast, and the back has one read (which side of the fullback's block to take). Iso was a staple of the
I-formation era, and it has faded with the fullback. In 2025 only about one NFL snap in ten came from personnel with two backs
(a fullback or a second running back), so most teams now lead a tight end or H-back through the hole instead, either as a
true iso from two- and three-tight-end groupings or as the insert block on inside zone ([zone insert](03-02-zone-running.qmd),
where the line zone-blocks instead of blocking the man on it).[^personnel]

## Toss, sweep and pin-and-pull: power goes outside

Everything so far hit between the tackles or just outside them. The gap family also has outside runs, and they are built from
the same parts: block down, pull, lead.

A [**toss**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-toss-sweep) is the quarterback pitching the ball underhand to a back who is
already moving toward the sideline; a **sweep** is any outside run with blockers leading the back around the corner, whether
the ball is pitched or handed off. The toss saves time: the back catches the ball two or three yards wider and already at speed,
instead of waiting for a handoff and then turning the corner.

### The ancestor: Lombardi's sweep

The most famous sweep in football is the **Packers sweep** of Vince Lombardi's Green Bay teams of the 1960s.

Guards Jerry Kramer and Fuzzy Thurston pulled in tandem, leading Paul Hornung or Jim Taylor around the end, and the play was the
cornerstone of an offense that won five NFL championships in seven seasons (1961, 1962, 1965, 1966 and 1967, the last two
including Super Bowls I and II).[^sweep] Lombardi's own phrase for the back's job became the title of his 1963 book, *Run to
Daylight*: the back did not run to a spot drawn on the card; he read the tight end's block on the outside linebacker and went
wherever the defender was not. Lombardi drilled the sweep endlessly precisely because everyone knew it was coming, and the
answer to "everyone knows" was perfect execution plus a back who could choose his hole late.

Look at @fig-packers-sweep with this chapter's vocabulary and you can see it is power stretched sideways: down blocks inside,
pullers leading, a fullback on the end, the backside left to chase. Why pitch or hand the ball wide at all, instead of
running power off-tackle? Because some defenses are strongest inside, and the sweep makes every defender run. The price is
time: the back is in the backfield longer, so a defender who beats a down block gets to him. The modern descendant is
pin-and-pull.

### Pin-and-pull

Outside zone ([03-02](03-02-zone-running.qmd)) has a problem against **wide fronts**, defenses whose ends line up well outside
the tackles and tight ends. To run outside zone, the play-side blockers must *reach* the defenders in front of them, getting
their heads to the outside, and a defender lined up two yards outside you is almost impossible to reach. Defenses that play wide
(a wide-9 end, an end in a wide 5, an outside linebacker walked out over the tight end) are partly built to kill the
reach.

[**Pin-and-pull**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pin-and-pull) gives up on reaching. Each lineman, backside ones included,
asks one question about the gap on his *backside*, the side away from the play:

- **Is a defender in it (or shaded into it)? Pin him.** Block down on him, which is an easy angle because he is inside you.
- **Is it empty? Pull.** Run around the blocks outside you and lead.

In @fig-pin-and-pull that sorts the whole line. The left tackle has the wide 5 in his backside gap and the center has the
1 shaded on his backside, so both pin; the right tackle has the 3 in his, so he pins; both guards have nobody in theirs,
so both pull. The tight end is the usual exception: in most versions he does not pull even with an empty backside gap
(somebody has to stop the play-side linebacker from running straight to the ball), so he goes inside to the Mike.

The beauty of the rule is that it turns the defense's alignment into the offense's advantage. The wider the defenders line up,
the more of them end up *inside* an offensive lineman, where he can pin them, and the more linemen are left uncovered, free to
pull. Every block in @fig-pin-and-pull is either a down block or a block by a puller with a running start, and nobody has to
reach anyone. The rules adjust to the front without a new call, the way zone rules do, which is why some coaches describe
pin-and-pull as a gap scheme that thinks like zone.[^pinpull]

::: {#cell-fig-pin-and-pull .cell execution_count=12}

go_to(p, "QB", (-2.4, 0.9), "path", speed=4.0)                             # reverse out and toss
go_to(p, "RB", (7.0, 6.2), "run", via=[(-5.6, 2.2), (-3.6, 5.0), (-0.6, 5.6)])

for k in ("LE", "NT", "DT"):
    say(f, p, 2.35, p.players[k].w, "pinned", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.4, weight="bold")
point_to(f, p, (-5.0, -4.6), (-1.0, -1.6), "empty backside\ngap: both guards\npull", color=PURPLE, fontsize=6.6)

The 2024 Washington Commanders, with Kliff Kingsbury calling plays for rookie Jayden Daniels, leaned on pin-and-pull as the

## The draw: a run disguised as a pass

The last member of the family barely looks like a run at all. On a [**draw play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draw-play)
(or simply a [**draw**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-draw)), the offensive line sets up as if to pass-protect, the quarterback
shows a drop, the pass rushers are allowed to run upfield, and the ball is handed to the back late, after the linebackers have
turned their backs to run to their pass-coverage zones. The rush has *drawn* the defenders out of the play.

::: {#cell-fig-draw .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def draw_play():
    """A shotgun draw against a four-man rush with the linebackers dropping into zones."""
    off = line() + [te(+1), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"),
                    O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
    dfn = [D("LE", "DL", 1.0, -5.0, "E"), dl("LT3", "3", -1), dl("RT3", "3", 1), D("RE", "DL", 1.0, 6.0, "E"),
           D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -2.2, "W"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 2.0, "M"),
           D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -9.0, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
           D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.0, "SS")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=11)
    # defense: four rush upfield, the linebackers drop to their zones
    go_to(p, "LE", (-3.6, -5.6), "path", speed=4.6)                    # wide, upfield rushes ...
    go_to(p, "RE", (-3.6, 6.2), "path", speed=4.6)
    go_to(p, "LT3", (-1.6, -2.7), "path", speed=2.6)                   # ... and the tackles get walled outside
    go_to(p, "RT3", (-1.6, 2.7), "path", speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (9.5, -3.6), "path", speed=4.4)                   # zone drops, backs to the ball
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (9.5, 3.4), "path", speed=4.4)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (8.6, -1.6), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25)       # ... then react, too late
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (8.6, 1.4), "path", speed=4.0, delay=0.25)
    go_to(p, "NB", (8.5, -9.5), "path", speed=4.0)
    for k in ("FS", "SS"):
        go_to(p, k, (14.5, p.players[k].w * 1.1), "path", speed=2.0)
    # offense: the line sets as if to pass, then rides the rushers past the ball
    go_to(p, "LT", (-3.0, -4.3), speed=3.0, via=[(-1.8, -3.9)])        # kick slide, ride him deep
    go_to(p, "RT", (-3.0, 4.4), speed=3.0, via=[(-1.8, 3.9)])
    go_to(p, "LG", (-2.0, -1.9), speed=2.2, via=[(-1.6, -1.6)])        # set, then turn the 3 out
    go_to(p, "RG", (-2.0, 1.9), speed=2.2, via=[(-1.6, 1.6)])
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.4, 0.0), speed=2.0)                              # sets, nobody comes ...
    go_to(p, "C", (7.5, -0.9), speed=5.0, delay=0.3)                   # ... so he climbs to the Will
    go_to(p, "Y", (7.9, 2.2), speed=4.2, via=[(1.5, 4.6)])             # releases, then blocks the Mike
    for k in ("X", "Z", "H"):
        p.route(k, [(0, 0), (13, 0)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-6.2, 0.2), "path", speed=3.0)                     # sells the drop
    go_to(p, "RB", (-5.5, 0.9), "run", speed=1.5)                      # steps up as if to protect
    go_to(p, "RB", (8.0, -0.4), "run", speed=6.2, delay=0.55, via=[(-5.9, 0.55), (-2.0, 0.2), (1.5, 0.0)])
    p.handoff("RB", t=0.95)
    return p


animation_or_strip(draw_play(), [0.0, 0.8, 1.45, 2.45], lateral=(-8.6, 8.6), window=(-7.4, 11.6), ncols=2,

A shotgun draw on third-and-11 against a four-man rush (simulated, BDB-format tracking; the yellow line is the line to gain; two safeties are 13 yards deep, above the picture). Watch the two linebackers (orange rings) run away from the ball while the line sets as if to pass. By frame 4 the guards have walled the 3-techniques outside, the center has climbed toward the Will and the Y toward the Mike, and the back (green ring) is through the A gap at linebackers nine yards deep.

The draw belongs in a gap chapter because it is built on the same principle as the trap: **let the defender go where he wants
to go, then block him there**. The guards in @fig-draw do not try to stop the 3-techniques from rushing; they let them come
upfield and then turn them outward, away from the A gaps. The tackles ride the ends wide and deep, the way they would on any
pass. The more eagerly the defense rushes the passer, the bigger the hole in the middle gets. And the linebackers, who on a
normal run would be the problem, have spent the first second running *away* from the ball to cover receivers.

That tells you when to expect it: on **passing downs, against a four-man rush with linebackers who drop**. Third-and-long is the
classic draw situation, and a defense with two deep safeties and two linebackers dropping into zones is the classic draw
defense.

Be honest about what it buys, though, because you have the tools from
[Downs, Distance and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd). A six-yard gain on
third-and-11 is a *failed* play by [success rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate): the offense punts anyway.
In the 2023–2025 regular seasons, NFL designed runs on third-and-10 to -12 converted about 12% of the time and averaged
about −0.29 [EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) a play; dropbacks in the same spot converted about 27% and averaged
about −0.11.[^thirdlong] Some of that gap is selection (offenses that have already given up on the down, late in a half or
protecting a lead, call runs), but the point stands: a third-and-long draw is usually a deliberate *conservative* choice.
Coaches call it to avoid a sack or an interception, to shorten the punt or set up a field-goal try, and to make the
pass rush hesitate a half-step on the next third down. Against a defense that drops its linebackers it is also, now and
then, a long run. It is rarely the best way to get eleven yards.

The trade: the draw is helpless against *interior* pressure. If a linebacker comes *forward* at the snap instead of
dropping, or walks up into an A gap before the snap, he is standing exactly where the play needs to go, and nobody is
assigned to him because the line is busy pretending to pass-block. A defense that sits a linebacker in the middle as a
[spy](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd) on a running quarterback ruins it for the same reason. Pressure
off the edge is a different story: an outside blitzer runs himself past the play, which is exactly what the draw wants.

Paul Brown's Browns made the draw famous in the late 1940s with Marion Motley, a fullback of about 232 to 238 pounds who could
also pass-block, which made the fake believable. One story says it began by accident, with Otto Graham improvising a handoff
on a broken pass play; another has Brown already experimenting with a delayed handoff to Motley in 1945. Either way it was a
Cleveland staple by the time the Browns joined the NFL in 1950.[^draw] Its descendants, the
quarterback draw and the run-pass option, belong to [Option Football](03-04-option-football.qmd) and
[RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd).

## The family on one page

Every play in this chapter answers the same two questions, *where do the extra blockers come from, and who is left
free?*, and each carries a rule the line can apply to whatever front it sees. @tbl-family puts them side by side, with
the holes in [03-01](03-01-run-game-language.qmd)'s gap letters. To draw any of these plays against a new front, start
from its rule column, not from a remembered picture.

| Play | Where it hits | The line's rule | Extra blockers | Left free |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Power | off-tackle: the C gap, or the D gap outside a tight end | gap, down, backer on the play side; center blocks back | backside guard leads; fullback or H-back kicks out | the backside end |
| Counter | off-tackle, like power | the same play-side rules; center blocks back | backside guard kicks out; tackle (or H-back) leads | the backside end, unless a tight end or H-back fills |
| Duo | A or B gap, decided by the Mike | doubles on both tackles, everyone else man-on; the doubles own the linebackers | none | nobody in a six-man box; the extra man in a bigger one |
| Trap | B gap, just inside the trapped tackle | let one lineman through; the man in front of him releases inside to a linebacker | backside guard, on a short pull | nobody, if the trap lands |
| Wham | like trap | like trap, but the guards climb | a tight end or H-back crossing | like trap |
| Iso | a bubble: an open gap with a linebacker behind it | block the man on you; the uncovered lineman takes the backside linebacker | fullback leads onto the play-side linebacker | the safeties |
| Sweep, pin-and-pull | outside the end man | pin the man in your backside gap, or pull if it is empty | both guards | usually a safety, and the backside chase |
| Draw | A gaps | pass set; wall the rushers away from the middle; center and tight end climb | none: the rushers take themselves out | any linebacker who does not drop |
